edges.title: Corelli climbs Couperin’s Parnassus

works.to: Le Parnasse, ou L’Apothéose de Corelli (1724)

edges.claim: Couperin’s 1724 trio sonata gives Corelli a programme in seven named movements: he petitions the Muses, drinks at Hippocrene, sleeps, and is placed beside Apollo. The tribute is explicit in the work’s title and movement headings, rather than a resemblance retrospectively assigned by listeners.

edges.title: Lully and Corelli reconcile on Parnassus
edges.claim: In Couperin’s 1725 instrumental homage, Apollo persuades Lully and Corelli to unite French and Italian tastes. Two successive headings specify Lully playing the subject with Corelli accompanying, then Corelli playing while Lully accompanies: stylistic reconciliation becomes an audible exchange of roles.

edges.title: An inherited dance closes Vivaldi’s first opus

works.from: The late Folia melody and harmonic scheme
works.to: Trio Sonata in D minor, Op. 1 No. 12, RV 63 (1705)

edges.claim: Vivaldi ended his first published collection of trio sonatas with variations on La Folia for two violins and continuo. The opening Adagio states the familiar D-minor melody before the changing tempi and figuration; the source is a shared tradition, not a tune invented by Corelli.
edges.note: The tradition node’s year 1600 is a display anchor, not an asserted origin date for La Folia.

edges.title: Voltaire supplies Rameau’s comédie-ballet
edges.claim: Rameau supplied the music for Voltaire’s La Princesse de Navarre in 1745. The comédie-ballet has an overture and three acts; its literary author is the same Voltaire better known for philosophical prose, not an anonymous court librettist.

edges.title: Bach outstays his leave in Lübeck
edges.claim: Bach obtained leave from his Arnstadt post in 1705 to visit Lübeck and hear Buxtehude, but remained away into 1706. The subsequent consistory examination records Bach’s explanation that he had travelled to learn things connected with his art: the encounter is supported by an employment dispute, not merely an influence legend.

edges.title: Frescobaldi’s organ Masses reach Bach’s desk

works.to: Bach’s study copy of Fiori musicali

edges.claim: A manuscript of Frescobaldi’s Fiori musicali bore Bach’s name and the date 1714; the volume was subsequently lost during the Second World War. The collection’s chant-based Kyrie versets, canzonas and ricercars gave him access to a specific Italian model of liturgical organ counterpoint, without requiring an invented chain of personal lessons from Frescobaldi to Bach.
edges.note: Older accounts call this Bach’s complete autograph copy. The 2026 source cautions that it may instead have been a scribal copy signed and dated by him; ‘copied’ here denotes manuscript transmission, not certainty about the copyist’s hand.

edges.title: Bach writes out a French organ book

works.to: Bach’s copy of Grigny’s organ collection

edges.claim: Bach’s autograph copy of Grigny’s Premier livre d’orgue survives in Frankfurt as Mus Hs 1538. In the same manuscript he copied Dieupart’s harpsichord suites and d’Anglebert’s ornament table: French repertory and instructions for playing its ornaments travelled together into his working library.
edges.note: The holding library dates the composite manuscript 1709–14, with catalogue metadata c. 1710. The timeline uses this approximate catalogue date, not the older claim that Bach copied Grigny in 1703.

edges.title: An ensemble sonata becomes a keyboard work
edges.claim: Bach’s A-minor keyboard Sonata BWV 965 adapts Reincken’s first sonata from Hortus musicus, originally ensemble music. The keyboard version retains a succession of introductory, fugal and dance movements: the transmission is an identifiable arrangement, not simply membership of the North German organ school.
edges.note: The date c. 1705 is approximate.

edges.title: Two solo violins move onto Bach’s organ

works.from: Concerto in A minor, Op. 3 No. 8, RV 522 (1711)
works.to: Organ Concerto in A minor, BWV 593 (c. 1713)

edges.claim: Bach transcribed Vivaldi’s A-minor concerto for two violins, strings and continuo as the solo-organ Concerto BWV 593 around 1713. The two manuals let him distinguish tutti and solo material; added ornaments, middle-voice detail and fuller chords adapt the same concerto architecture to the organ.
edges.note: The transcription is documented; c. 1713 is an approximate date, and Prince Johann Ernst’s precise role in supplying the print remains a probability.

edges.title: Four violins become four harpsichords

works.from: Concerto in B minor, Op. 3 No. 10, RV 580
works.to: Concerto for four harpsichords in A minor, BWV 1065 (c. 1730)

edges.claim: Bach converted Vivaldi’s B-minor concerto for four violins into an A-minor concerto for four harpsichords and strings. Each violin line becomes a two-handed keyboard part; the broken-chord slow movement remains especially close to Vivaldi’s original, despite the changed instrumental sound.
edges.note: Around 1730 is an estimate. The often-imagined performance by Bach and three of his children is not established and is not asserted here.

sources.title: Netherlands Bach Society: Concerto for four harpsichords, BWV 1065
sources.locator: ‘More and better’; work details and discussion of unknown origins

edges.title: An oboe concerto becomes keyboard ornament study

works.from: Oboe Concerto in D minor, S D935
works.to: Keyboard Concerto in D minor, BWV 974 (c. 1713–14)

edges.claim: The source of Bach’s BWV 974 is the D-minor oboe concerto by Alessandro Marcello, not his brother Benedetto. Bach recast the oboe-and-strings texture for one keyboard, preserving its Italian identity while elaborating the ornamented solo line.
edges.note: The transcription is dated approximately 1713–14; the route by which the manuscript reached Weimar is uncertain.

sources.title: Netherlands Bach Society: Concerto in D minor, BWV 974
sources.locator: ‘From oboe to keyboard’; catalogue details

edges.title: A Stabat mater becomes a German psalm
edges.claim: Bach adapted Pergolesi’s Stabat mater to a German paraphrase of Psalm 51 in Tilge, Höchster, meine Sünden, BWV 1083. The music crosses both language and liturgical context: a Latin Marian text gives way to a German penitential psalm.
edges.note: 1746 is a timeline anchor within the alternative 1744–48 and 1745–47 datings reported by the source; no exact first-performance date is claimed.

sources.title: Bach Cantatas Website: Psalm 51, BWV 1083
sources.locator: Work details: composition, adaptation and text

edges.title: Luther’s hymn becomes a contrapuntal fortress

works.from: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott
works.to: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott, BWV 80, Leipzig versions

edges.claim: Bach expanded an earlier Weimar cantata into a Leipzig Reformation cantata using Luther’s Ein feste Burg. In the opening movement the chorale appears in long notes in the instrumental parts while the chorus works around it in imitation; the hymn supplies a structural layer, not just a closing quotation.
edges.note: The Leipzig work developed in stages; 1730 is an approximate timeline anchor, not a fixed premiere date. Wilhelm Friedemann Bach’s later trumpet additions are not treated as his father’s original scoring.

sources.title: Craig Smith, Emmanuel Music: BWV 80 notes
sources.locator: Weimar-to-Leipzig revision history and opening motet chorus

edges.title: An old Credo intonation enters Bach’s counterpoint

works.from: Plainchant intonation, Credo in unum Deum
works.to: Mass in B minor, BWV 232, opening Credo

edges.claim: Bach based the opening of the B-minor Mass’s Credo on an older chant intonation for the words Credo in unum Deum. He gives the borrowed head-motif measured rhythm and sets it over a walking continuo bass, joining an archaic vocal subject to an active instrumental foundation.
edges.note: 1749 marks the approximate completion of the assembled Mass, not a securely dated first invention of this movement. The tradition node’s year 800 is only a timeline anchor, not an origin date for this particular melody.

edges.title: Couperin enters the Bach family notebook

works.from: Les Bergeries, Second livre, Sixième ordre (1717)
works.to: Anna Magdalena Bach’s 1725 notebook, No. 6, BWV Anh. 183

edges.claim: The rondeau in B♭ major entered as No. 6 in the 1725 Anna Magdalena notebook is Couperin’s Les Bergeries, published in 1717. Its presence documents French harpsichord music in the Bach household, but does not make the piece Bach’s composition or establish him as this entry’s copyist.
edges.note: The year names the notebook; not every entry was necessarily written in 1725. ‘Copied’ describes household transmission, not an authenticated Johann Sebastian autograph.

sources.locator: Anh. III 183, No. 6; introduction to the 1725 notebook’s several scribes

edges.title: Zachow joins counterpoint to foreign repertory
edges.claim: Handel studied with the Halle organist Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow before his later Hamburg apprenticeship. Zachow’s teaching combined counterpoint and figured bass with exposure to Italian and French instrumental music, an unusually concrete basis for Handel’s later command of several national styles.
edges.note: 1693 is an approximate childhood timeline anchor. The cited scholarly account explicitly qualifies details inherited from Mainwaring’s retrospective biography.

sources.title: David Kimbell, Handel on the Stage, chapter 1
sources.locator: pp. 2–3: Halle, Zachow and Mainwaring’s evidence

edges.title: Milton’s opposed poems alternate inside Handel’s ode

works.to: L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato (1740)

edges.claim: Charles Jennens selected and interleaved passages from Milton’s companion poems for Handel’s L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato, first performed in London on 27 February 1740. The third part, Il Moderato, is Jennens’s addition, not a third Milton poem: literary adaptation is built into the musical alternation of temperaments.

sources.title: Martin Pearlman, Boston Baroque: Handel’s L’Allegro
sources.locator: Work details and ‘The libretto’

edges.title: Dryden’s musical feast reaches Covent Garden

works.from: Alexander’s Feast, or the Power of Musick

edges.claim: The Covent Garden advertisement for 19 February 1736 announces a new ode written by the late Dryden and set by Handel. A letter of 24 January already describes Handel playing almost the entire new work to Shaftesbury, who singled out the chorus beginning ‘Happy, happy’: contemporary witnesses identify both the literary source and the composition in preparation.

sources.title: Handel Reference Database, 1736: contemporary letters and advertisements
sources.locator: 24 January: Shaftesbury to Harris; 19 February: Covent Garden advertisement

edges.title: A Roman keyboard contest survives as anecdote
edges.claim: The familiar account places Handel and Scarlatti in a keyboard contest at Cardinal Ottoboni’s in Rome, with Handel preferred on the organ. The story belongs to the retrospective anecdotal tradition surrounding their Italian encounters; it is evidence of how their reputations were narrated, not proof that a particular Scarlatti sonata borrows from Handel.
edges.note: The exact date, judging and details are not secured by contemporary contest documentation in the sources consulted. Sandra Dolby explains the second-hand, orally transmitted character of Mainwaring’s Italian anecdotes; 1708 follows the cited concise biography, not a verified event record.

sources.title: Domenico Scarlatti: a concise biography
sources.locator: Ottoboni meetings and the reported 1708 competition

edges.title: Emanuel identifies his only music teacher

works.to: C. P. E. Bach’s training in keyboard and composition

edges.claim: In the autobiography prepared for Burney and published in 1773, Emanuel Bach identifies his father as his only teacher of composition and keyboard playing. The same document lists his first published keyboard minuet in 1731; the teaching link rests on the pupil’s own testimony, not merely their surname.
edges.note: 1731 anchors the end of the early-training period to Emanuel’s first listed publication, not the beginning or end of all lessons.

sources.title: C. P. E. Bach, Autobiography, translated and introduced by Paul Corneilson
sources.locator: Autobiography pp. 1 and 3, PDF pp. 5 and 7

edges.title: Haydn learns at the keyboard from Emanuel

works.from: C. P. E. Bach’s keyboard sonatas

edges.claim: Haydn recalled playing Emanuel Bach’s sonatas repeatedly during his early years of independent study. The testimony names actual keyboard works as models; it does not say that Haydn was Emanuel’s personal pupil or identify one particular sonata as the source of a later Haydn theme.
edges.note: The exact year and sonata volume are not established by the testimony reproduced here; 1750 is an approximate early-career anchor.

sources.title: Louis Nohl, Life of Haydn, reproducing Haydn’s recollections
sources.locator: Chapter I, pp. 28–29: purchase and repeated study of Emanuel Bach’s sonatas

edges.title: Palestrina becomes a counterpoint teacher on paper

works.from: Palestrina’s reputation as a contrapuntal model

edges.claim: Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum presents counterpoint through a dialogue between Aloysius, representing Palestrina, and Josephus, representing Fux. The imagined lesson became a route from the older contrapuntal ideal into the studies of Haydn and Beethoven; it is not a historical claim that Fux met Palestrina.

sources.title: Fundación Gustavo Bueno: Fux, Gradus ad Parnassum, 1725 facsimile guide

edges.title: Haydn works Fux’s problems more than once
edges.claim: Griesinger’s account, reproduced by Nohl, describes Haydn solving Fux’s counterpoint problems, putting them aside, then returning to check them. The method was repeated written work rather than a single encounter with a famous treatise, and Haydn retained a worn copy.
edges.note: The study belongs to Haydn’s early independent years; 1750 is an approximate timeline anchor, not a dated exercise manuscript.

sources.title: Louis Nohl, Life of Haydn, citing Griesinger’s Biographical Notices
sources.locator: Chapter II, pp. 43–44, study of Fux and repeated revision of exercises

edges.title: Accompanying singing lessons teaches Haydn declamation

works.from: Porpora’s vocal and compositional teaching in Vienna

edges.claim: In Vienna, Haydn accompanied pupils in Porpora’s singing lessons and received instruction in return. Porpora’s teaching connected composition with singing and Italian declamation, a practical complement to Haydn’s independent keyboard and counterpoint studies.
edges.note: 1753 is an approximate placement within the early-1750s association; the sources give slightly different ranges for Porpora’s Vienna residence.

sources.title: Louis Nohl, Life of Haydn

edges.title: Haydn hears Handel’s London festival scale

works.from: Handel’s music at the London commemoration

edges.claim: During his first London visit, Haydn attended the Handel commemoration at the end of May 1791. Hearing Handel’s choral music in this setting preceded Haydn’s later English-inspired oratorios; the encounter is firmer evidence than treating every large Haydn chorus as a borrowing from Messiah.

sources.title: Louis Nohl, Life of Haydn: first London visit
sources.locator: pp. 119–121, end-of-May Handel festival in the 1791 narrative

edges.title: Haydn hears Mozart’s new quartets at home
edges.claim: Mozart played his six new quartets for Haydn in Vienna on 15 January 1785; the newest three were heard again at Mozart’s home on 12 February. Leopold’s report of the second gathering preserves Haydn’s strong approval, documenting direct listening rather than an inferred general kinship between their quartet styles.

sources.title: Neue Mozart-Ausgabe VIII/20/1/2: String Quartets, foreword by Ludwig Finscher
sources.locator: p. IX: 15 January and 12 February 1785; Leopold’s February letter

edges.title: Six quartets are entrusted to Haydn

works.to: Dedication to Joseph Haydn in Artaria’s 1785 edition

edges.claim: Artaria’s first edition of Mozart’s six quartets carries an Italian dedication to Haydn. The dedication is a separate piece of evidence from possible Op. 33 modelling: it is an explicit published acknowledgement, while the precise extent of that musical modelling is left open in the critical edition’s foreword.

sources.title: Neue Mozart-Ausgabe VIII/20/1/2: foreword and first-edition facsimiles
sources.locator: pp. VII and X; facsimiles 5–6, p. XVII

edges.title: Bach’s keyboard sonatas become Mozart concertos
edges.claim: Mozart’s three concertos K. 107 transform Johann Christian Bach’s Op. 5 Nos. 2, 3 and 4 into works for keyboard with strings. The surviving manuscript contains work by both Wolfgang and Leopold, so these arrangements document a practical family workshop in concerto writing as well as Wolfgang’s admiration for the London Bach.
edges.note: 1771 is an approximate placement: the NMA dates the manuscript no earlier than the end of 1770 and probably later, rather than fixing a single composition year.

edges.title: Emanuel’s miniature supplies a concerto finale

works.from: La Boehmer, published in Musikalisches Allerley (1761)
works.to: Keyboard Concerto in D major, K. 40, finale (July 1767)

edges.claim: The finale of Mozart’s K. 40 reworks Emanuel Bach’s keyboard piece La Boehmer. Leopold dated the concerto manuscript July 1767, and the critical edition identifies this specific source: the Bach connection here is an actual pasticcio movement, not a general claim about Mozart’s expressive style.

edges.title: Bach’s keyboard fugues acquire string voices

works.to: Five fugues for string quartet, K. 405 (1782)

edges.claim: Mozart arranged five Bach fugues for two violins, viola and cello in the group traditionally numbered K. 405. The critical edition places the Bach arrangements beside the quartet work of 1782; the arrangement itself is secure evidence of study, without proving that every later contrapuntal Mozart passage came from Bach.

edges.title: Sunday sessions bring Bach and Handel home

works.from: Van Swieten’s Bach and Handel repertory
works.to: Mozart’s Prelude and Fugue in C, K. 394 (1782)

edges.claim: In his letter to Nannerl of 20 April 1782, Mozart explains that van Swieten lent him Bach and Handel works after he had played them at the baron’s Sunday gatherings. Constanze’s enthusiasm for fugues then helped prompt the Prelude and Fugue K. 394: the letter supplies a named intermediary and a particular compositional result.

edges.title: Mozart recolours Messiah for Viennese winds
edges.claim: At van Swieten’s initiative, Mozart arranged Handel’s Messiah for German-language performances in Vienna in 1789. His version adds wind colouring to Handel’s texture rather than composing a new oratorio; the arrangement was made for particular performances and appeared in print only after Mozart’s death.

edges.title: A Mozart suite looks towards Handel
edges.claim: The critical edition identifies Handel’s suites as the principal stylistic model for Mozart’s incomplete Suite K. 399. Its overture, allemande and courante belong to Mozart’s 1782 engagement with older keyboard music; the unfinished sarabande also prevents the fragment from being presented as a completed four-movement suite.
edges.note: The model is the critical editor’s stylistic attribution, supported by Nissen’s annotation on the autograph; Mozart did not leave a statement naming a specific Handel suite as his source.

edges.title: Haydn teaches Beethoven counterpoint in Vienna

works.from: Haydn’s counterpoint teaching, based on Fux

edges.claim: Beethoven’s lessons with Haydn began in early 1793 after his move from Bonn to Vienna. The exercises drew on Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum; when Haydn left for London in January 1794, Beethoven continued contrapuntal study with Albrechtsberger.

edges.title: Fugue and canon follow Haydn’s departure

works.from: Albrechtsberger’s teaching of counterpoint, fugue and canon

edges.claim: After Haydn’s January 1794 departure for London, Beethoven took lessons from Johann Georg Albrechtsberger. The subjects were counterpoint, fugue and canon, making this a different documented stage of training from the Italian vocal work he later undertook with Salieri.

sources.title: Beethoven-Haus Bonn: Beethoven on postage stamps

edges.title: Salieri teaches Beethoven Italian vocal style

works.from: Salieri’s instruction in Italian vocal writing

edges.claim: Beethoven studied Italian vocal and operatic style with Antonio Salieri around 1800–02. These lessons concerned writing for the voice, rather than replacing the counterpoint training Beethoven had already received from Haydn and Albrechtsberger.
edges.note: The museum gives the lesson period approximately, not as an uninterrupted daily course.

edges.title: Beethoven copies fugues to teach an archduke

works.from: Gradus ad Parnassum: two four-part fugues
works.to: Beethoven’s autograph study material, HCB Mh 45

edges.claim: Beethoven’s autograph HCB Mh 45 copies two four-part fugues from Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum. Beethoven-Haus relates the copy, probably, to the compendium he prepared for Archduke Rudolph’s theoretical lessons: the older textbook passes through Beethoven to another pupil.
edges.note: The copying is documented; its intended use for Rudolph is probable, not certain. 1809 anchors the beginning of Rudolph’s theoretical tuition, not an exact date written on these leaves.

edges.title: The Well-Tempered Clavier enters Beethoven’s early training
edges.claim: Neefe’s communication to Cramer’s Magazin der Musik, dated 2 March 1783, identifies Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier as central to the young Beethoven’s keyboard repertory and says Neefe supplied it. The same report describes instruction in thoroughbass and composition, locating Bach’s music inside Beethoven’s practical education rather than merely linking two later reputations for fugue.
edges.note: Neefe’s promotional report establishes substantial use of the collection, not mastery of every prelude and fugue in both books. Its statement that Beethoven was eleven is not repeated as a correct age.

edges.title: Beethoven copies Emanuel while studying with Haydn

works.from: C. P. E. Bach’s keyboard sonatas and Versuch

edges.claim: During his Viennese studies in 1793–94, Beethoven copied keyboard sonatas by Emanuel Bach. Other surviving extracts come from Emanuel’s Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, which Beethoven also used when teaching his own pupils.

edges.title: Handel’s conquering hero becomes chamber variations

works.from: See, the conqu’ring hero comes, Judas Maccabaeus
works.to: Twelve Variations for cello and piano, WoO 45 (1796)

edges.claim: Beethoven used Handel’s ‘See, the conqu’ring hero comes’ as the theme of twelve variations for cello and piano, WoO 45, in 1796. His surviving study copies also include passages from Handel’s Messiah in Mozart’s arrangement: borrowing a recognisable tune and copying a score are two separately documented forms of his engagement with Handel.

edges.title: Beethoven studies Mozart’s ensembles for Fidelio

works.to: Beethoven’s study copy during work on Fidelio

edges.claim: While beginning work on Fidelio, Beethoven copied passages from Mozart’s Don Giovanni to study the handling of vocal ensembles. Beethoven-Haus exhibited this study manuscript: the mechanism is written compositional analysis, not the unverified story that Mozart personally taught Beethoven in 1787.
edges.note: 1805 is the first-version Fidelio anchor, not a claimed exact date on the study copy.

edges.title: Schiller’s ode enters a symphonic finale
edges.claim: Beethoven incorporated Schiller’s An die Freude in the choral finale of the Ninth Symphony, first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824. The literary connection belongs to the sung finale, not to a retrospective programme imposed on the instrumental movements.

sources.title: Beethoven-Haus Bonn: Beethoven on postage stamps
sources.locator: ‘The Ninth Premiered in Vienna (1824)’

edges.title: Goethe’s tragedy receives Beethoven’s stage music
edges.claim: Beethoven composed music for Goethe’s Egmont in 1809–10, including songs, entr’actes and music for the tragedy’s final act. He announced the work to Goethe by letter in 1811, before their personal meetings in 1812; the setting therefore did not result from a collaboration begun at Teplitz.

sources.title: Beethoven-Haus Bonn and Goethe-Schiller-Archiv: My harmony linked to yours
sources.locator: p. 2, ‘Egmont’, cases 7–9; ‘Personal Encounter’

edges.title: Schubert’s early compositions lead to Salieri lessons
edges.claim: Schubert’s early compositional gifts led to study with Antonio Salieri in Vienna. The link joins Schubert to a working vocal composer and teacher, rather than to the fictional account of Salieri as Mozart’s murderer.
edges.note: 1812 is an approximate conventional start-year anchor; the cited overview establishes the teaching relationship without dating every lesson.

sources.title: Christopher H. Gibbs, Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center: Franz Schubert
sources.locator: ‘Early Years: The Prince of Song’

edges.title: Faust’s spinning scene becomes a piano song
edges.claim: Schubert set Goethe’s Gretchen text as Gretchen am Spinnrade, D. 118, in 1814. Gibbs places it beside Erlkönig among the early Goethe settings that made the piano an active interpreter of the poem, rather than treating it as a neutral support for the voice.

sources.title: Christopher H. Gibbs: Franz Schubert, Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center

edges.title: Goethe’s ballad becomes Schubert’s first published opus
edges.claim: Schubert composed his setting of Goethe’s Erlkönig, D. 328, in 1815; it later became his Op. 1. The pairing of a specific poem, catalogue number and publication identity makes this a direct literary inheritance, not a loose association with German Romantic poetry.

sources.locator: ‘Early Years’: Erlkönig, D. 328, Op. 1 (1815)

edges.title: Spanish strumming enters a keyboard sonata

works.to: Keyboard Sonata in A minor, K. 175

edges.claim: Giulio d’Amore’s Santa Cecilia programme note hears Andalusian guitar attack and dance energy in the dense, dissonant chords of Scarlatti’s K. 175. This is a stylistic reading of music written for keyboard, not evidence that Scarlatti quoted a recoverable folk tune or originally composed the sonata for guitar.
edges.note: The cultural model is a critical interpretation, not a documented commission or named melodic source. The year 1752 dates the principal Venice manuscript copy, not necessarily composition; the tradition node’s year 1700 is only a display anchor.

edges.title: Schubert carries a torch for Beethoven
edges.claim: Schubert was a torchbearer in Beethoven’s funeral procession on 29 March 1827. This public act of homage is documented separately from uncertain stories of bedside visits, and does not imply that the two men had enjoyed a sustained personal friendship.
